messages.subject: Chains mixing poorly when fitting power law
parts:
I fit a power law to my data (y = a * x^b). The resulting chain (especially from cmdstan doesn't look good, see attached csv file that contains the posterior dists extracted from the output file of cmdstan (columns sdPow, aPow and bPow).

When using rstan, there are less such areas where no sampling takes place, but still not the best mixing (a small part of the posterior is a flat line (see traceplot)


My .stan file (pow.stan):

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[N] x;
  vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
  real a;
  real b;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  real mu;
 
  a  ~ uniform(0, 200);
  b ~ uniform(0, 2);

 
 
  for (i in 1:N)
    {
    mu <- a * x[i]^b;
    y[i] ~ normal(mu, sigma);
    }
}

The data:
x <- c(80,1,16,44,24,80,1)
y <- c(1000,10,140,450,250,1000,10)
N <- 7

dat <- list(N = length(x), y = y,x = x)

fit2 <- stan(file = 'pow.stan', data = dat,
             iter = 5000, chains = 1,warmup = 1000)

traceplot(fit2)

parts:
RStan and CmdStan produce the same answers for the same random seed.

In addition to the reasons Krzysztof mentions, the uniform priors are almost
certainly bad news computationally and statistically if there is probability
mass near the boundaries.

For efficiency, it's best to compute the entire vector of mu values
(as a local) then call normal once with vectorization. It cuts down on
the number of interpreted autodiff calls internally.

Also, you don't have much data, which means the priors are even more
important.

I only saw a .csv file attached.

- Bob

First, I'd listen to whatever Aki has to say.

But to answer the simple Stan question, no it won't
lead to rejected proposals.

If you have

real<lower=0> b
...
b ~ normal(1, 1);

then what you get is the normal(1, 1) truncated below at 0.
The normalizing term for the truncation is a constant, so
we don't need it. The constraint will automatically do a log
transform to where the real sampling is happening in the
unconstrained space.

- Bob

I'm curious, why don't you use power law distribution? In your model the variance of the data is homoskedastic, which does not usually hold for power law distributed data.
I got good mixing with Generalized Pareto distribution https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/generalized$20pareto/stan-users/C6IxqRU1Cuw/WyPUhdUOBQAJ

Aki

On Friday, March 11, 2016 at 2:41:53 PM UTC+2, Ulf Mertens wrote:
I fit a power law to my data (y = a * x^b). The resulting chain (especially from cmdstan doesn't look good, see attached csv file that contains the posterior dists extracted from the output file of cmdstan (columns sdPow, aPow and bPow).

When using rstan, there are less such areas where no sampling takes place, but still not the best mixing (a small part of the posterior is a flat line (see traceplot)


My .stan file (pow.stan):

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[N] x;
  vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
  real a;
  real b;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  real mu;
 
  a  ~ uniform(0, 200);
  b ~ uniform(0, 2);

 
 
  for (i in 1:N)
    {
    mu <- a * x[i]^b;
    y[i] ~ normal(mu, sigma);
    }
}

The data:
x <- c(80,1,16,44,24,80,1)
y <- c(1000,10,140,450,250,1000,10)
N <- 7

dat <- list(N = length(x), y = y,x = x)

fit2 <- stan(file = 'pow.stan', data = dat,
             iter = 5000, chains = 1,warmup = 1000)

traceplot(fit2)
